A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AICrypto benchmark and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched despite the changed format and appendix organization.

before.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of 17 LLMs on MCQs, CTF challenges, and proof problems, together with human comparisons and model-output case studies.

after.justification: v5 reports revised benchmark evaluations and additional original experiments measuring automated graders' agreement with human scores.

M1.justification: v3 relies on manual proof grading after finding LLM grading unreliable. v5 Section 3.4 adopts an automated component using GPT-5.1 and Gemini-3-Pro-Preview, each conditioned on the problem, reference solution, rubric, and submitted proof, with six ratings averaged. This substantially changes the benchmark's grading procedure; the CTF agent remains.

E1.justification: The 135 MCQs and 150 CTF challenges remain, with existing categories merged in Figure 1. Proof problems increase from 18 to 30 and include homework, but the PDFs do not map the complete problem sets or explain whether the former SIGN problem was removed or reclassified. Changes in substantive coverage beyond sample counts and regrouping cannot be established reliably.

E2.justification: v5 Appendix F/Table 4 introduces a substantial comparison of proof-scoring methods: the six-rating mean against two trimmed means, voting, and each grader's individual mean. v3 contains no corresponding evaluated comparator set. The principal 17-model solver lineup is largely retained.

E3.justification: Proof evaluation changes from 18 exam problems with original point weights and manual grading to 30 uniformly weighted five-point problems, reporting the best total score across three runs divided by 150. Homework problems are evaluated independently, while exam dialogue is retained. The reported Gemini solver identifier also changes from gemini-2.5-pro-preview-06-05 to gemini-2.5-pro.

E4.justification: v5 adds aggregation and individual-versus-combined-grader ablations testing agreement with human marks (Table 4). It removes the CTF iteration/success analysis in v3 Figure 15. Appendix case studies also change: the dynamic example switches from hash preimages to a modulus oracle, the failed example switches from RSA to a singular-curve knapsack, and Gemini's failed OWF proof is omitted.

E5.justification: v5 first specifies three proof-generation runs and three independent ratings from each of two graders. It adds Pearson/Spearman correlations and significance reporting, with all reported p-values below 10^-10. The three CTF attempts were already documented in v3. The grading-validation sample count is inconsistent: 306 in Section 2.5 versus 307 in Section 3.4.

E6.justification: Figure 8 replaces proof results under the revised protocol: human scores change from 88.1% to 94.0%, and o3-high from 84.2% to 82.9%. Figure 14 changes GPT-4.1 MCQ accuracy from 92.6% to 89.6%. The Gemini CTF entry changes from 55.3% for the preview model to 56.0% for the later identifier. Table 4 adds grader-correlation results. The proof and Gemini differences are not controlled same-setting performance gains or losses.

T1.justification: The sample Gemini proof in v3 Appendix G.1 is replaced in v5 Appendix I.1: its PRG construction changes from ignoring an input bit to modifying two fixed seeds, with a different security argument. Gemini's failed OWF construction is removed. These are changes to mathematical examples; the displayed problem statements and retained o3 proofs remain substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: v5's abstract and introduction promote validated automated proof grading, detailed rubrics, and reference solutions as a core contribution. v3 instead foregrounds the CTF agent and relies on human proof assessment. The benchmark contribution now includes 30 proof problems. Broad claims about strong basic knowledge and weaknesses in complex reasoning remain.

C2.justification: v3 identifies unreliable automated proof judging as a limitation requiring human grading; v5 interprets its correlations as evidence of effective automation and removes that limitation. v5 adds an explicit MCQ-saturation limitation and argues that the proof questions may indicate research-level reasoning ability. The earlier ENC-versus-FUN interpretation and interpretation of Claude's persistence are removed.

D1.justification: v5 supplies an example five-point grading rubric (Figure 6), grader prompts and input templates, and conditional versus parallel scoring rules (Appendix J.1, Figures 26–27). Table 2 newly documents 546 person-hours of benchmark preparation. v3 mentions grading criteria but lacks these operational details. Existing CTF hardware, software, and repository-access information are largely retained.

R1.justification: v5 adds structured benchmark positioning in Table 1, including Shao et al. (2024a) and InterCode-CTF. New citations cover MATH, Luong et al.'s automated grading, ReAct, and the grader models. Existing programming-related work moves intact to Appendix B, and the broader research positioning remains.

P1.justification: The title is shortened and numerous passages and cross-references are edited. The expert panel moves from Section 3.5 to Section 2.1, programming-related work moves to Appendix B, and failure-analysis sections are consolidated. Much existing exposition and prompting text is retained, with restructuring concentrated around the substantive grading additions.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one column to two, with extensive figure reflow. Heatmap categories are consolidated and Figure 14 loses its human columns. v5 adds benchmark, expert-effort, and grader-comparison tables, expands Figure 6 with a rubric, adds grader-prompt figures, and removes the CTF iteration plot.

improvement.justification: v5 improves the transparency and practicality of proof assessment through explicit grading instructions, prompts, and quantitative human-agreement validation, addressing v3's manual-grading bottleneck. Benefits are tempered by removed CTF iteration analysis and human MCQ breakdowns, plus new reporting inconsistencies: 306 versus 307 grading samples, and Section 4.2 claiming perfect o3 symmetric/Misc scores while Figure 14 reports 97.6% and 94.3%.
